prompt: `kubectl get secret db -o jsonpath="{.data}"` showed `bGFiLW9ubHktN0hxMg==`. What protects that value from somebody who can run that command?

choices.text: Nothing
choices.why: Right. Base64 is an encoding; anyone who can read the object can read the value.

choices.text: The base64 encoding, which needs the cluster's key
choices.why: Base64 has no key; one command reversed it.

choices.text: Encryption at rest, which is on by default
choices.why: It is off by default, and it protects copies of etcd, not readers of the API.

choices.text: The `tmpfs` the Secret is mounted on
choices.why: That protects the node's disk, not the API.

prompt: Why is the Secret volume in the pod a `tmpfs`?
hint: Where does a tmpfs keep its files?

choices.text: So the pod can write new secrets into it
choices.why: It was mounted read-only.

choices.text: Because Secrets are larger than ConfigMaps
choices.why: Both share the same one-mebibyte limit.

choices.text: So the value stays in the node's memory
choices.why: Right. A disk that is replaced or copied carries nothing.

choices.text: Because tmpfs encrypts its contents
choices.why: It does not; it keeps them in memory.

prompt: A service reads its database password from the variable `DB_PASSWORD`. A crash report it sends to an external tool includes the process environment. What does this lesson recommend?
hint: Which delivery is read only when the program chooses?

choices.text: Encode the variable in base64 twice
choices.why: Any encoding is reversed by whoever reads the report.

choices.text: Read it from a mounted file instead
choices.why: Right. A file is not inherited, dumped or listed in `/proc` with the environment.

choices.text: Turn on encryption at rest
choices.why: That protects etcd's copy; the leak here is from the running process.

choices.text: Mark the Secret immutable
choices.why: Immutability stops edits; it hides nothing.

prompt: Before encryption at rest, `strings` on the stored value showed `lab-only-7Hq2`. Who could read that?
hint: Think of copies of etcd's data.

choices.text: Only the API server
choices.why: Anything that reads etcd's data reads it, including a backup file.

choices.text: Nobody, because etcd encrypts everything it writes to its disk
choices.why: The plain text was right there.

choices.text: Anyone holding a copy of etcd's data, such as a leaked backup
choices.why: Right. That is the case encryption at rest exists for.

choices.text: Every pod in the cluster
choices.why: Pods reach the API server, not etcd.

prompt: After the API server was given the encryption configuration, `strings | grep -c lab-only` still printed `1`. Why?
hint: When does a value get encrypted?

choices.text: The flag needs a reboot of the node
choices.why: The API server restarted on its own when its manifest changed.

choices.text: Only new writes are encrypted, and it was old
choices.why: Right. Replacing every Secret with itself rewrote them, and the count went to 0.

choices.text: `identity` was listed first, so nothing is encrypted
choices.why: `secretbox` was first; `identity` was last, for reading old data.

choices.text: grep found the string in the key name
choices.why: The key is called `password`; the count was the value.

prompt: With encryption at rest on, `kubectl get secret db` still returned the password. Is the encryption broken?

choices.text: Yes; the value should come back encrypted
choices.why: The API server decrypts on the way out for anyone allowed to read it.

choices.text: Yes; secretbox only works on new clusters
choices.why: It worked here; etcd held `k8s:enc:secretbox:v1:key1:`.

choices.text: No; kubectl reads etcd directly and has the key
choices.why: kubectl never talks to etcd; only the API server does.

choices.text: No; it protects copies of the data, while API readers are RBAC's job
choices.why: Right. The two protections answer different worries.

prompt: After encryption at rest, the stored value began with `k8s:enc:___:v1:key1:`, naming the provider that encrypted it.
hint: The first provider in the list.

prompt: Match each worry with what protects against it.
hint: The table at the end of the lesson.

pairs.left: Somebody reads the Secret through the API
pairs.right: RBAC rules on who may get Secrets

pairs.left: A copy of etcd's data leaks
The value leaks from the running process
pairs.right: A file in a tmpfs instead of a variable
